scenario: AITA for keeping my son during my visitation instead of giving in to his mother? | I guess some backstory is due here. My ex and I have an 8 year old son, and we have been split up for a few years now. I have every other weekend parenting time along with a day during the week. It’s not enough time for me, but it’s what was legally decided through court. Her and I do not have the best relationship currently because I feel like I’m always being taken advantage of and I allow it because she always uses the “it’s for your son” excuse. I cherish my time with my son, but for the longest time, I allowed my ex to alter the parenting schedule to suit my son’s needs, whether for activities or family or if he just wasn’t feeling well. I always tried to be as accommodating as possible, even if it meant I didn’t see him for a week or more. Anyway, last Wednesday I was supposed to get him overnight, his mother called me and I asked if he could stay there since his cousin from out of town was staying with them. I reluctantly agreed but told her I wanted to get him Thursday instead. She agreed, and when Thursday came around, I texted her after work and said I was on my way to get him. She said they weren’t home, and I had to press her for information why. She decided to take the kids to a lake and said I needed to stop being grumpy because my son was having fun. We argued back and forth and since I did not drive all the way out to the lake to get him when I shouldn’t have had to in the first place, I told her that we should switch weekends (last weekend was hers, this one is mine) so that I had my make up time and his activities with her that fell on my weekend wouldn’t be interrupted. She refused, so now that my weekend is coming up, I’m not getting him at my regular time today because he’s at an amusement park with her family, and I am expected to give up even more of my valuable time tomorrow for their annual 4th of July party. Am I the asshole for putting my foot down and keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time?

However, as you've acknowledged, this approach is not immune to mistakes. Some potential pitfalls to consider: 1. **Information overload**: With the vast amount of information available, it can be challenging to discern what's relevant and accurate, potentially leading to misinformation or confusion. 2. **Bias and confirmation bias**: You may unintentionally seek out information that confirms your existing beliefs, rather than challenging them, which can limit your understanding and lead to biased decision-making. 3. **Lack of absolute moral framework**: Without a fixed moral framework, you may struggle with moral ambiguity or gray areas, potentially leading to uncertainty or inconsistent decision-making. 4. **Overreliance on human opinion**: While trusted individuals can provide valuable insights, their opinions may not always be objective or infallible, which can lead to mistakes if you rely too heavily on their perspectives. To mitigate these risks, consider the following strategies: 1. **Seek out diverse, credible sources**: Expose yourself to a wide range of perspectives and information from reputable sources to minimize the influence of bias and misinformation. 2. **Engage in reflective practice**: Regularly reflect on your decision-making processes and consider alternative perspectives to ensure you're not falling into patterns of confirmation bias. 3. **Develop a personal moral compass**: While you may not rely on religious texts, you can still develop a personal set of values and principles to guide your decision-making, helping you navigate complex situations. 4. **Cultivate empathy and self-awareness**: Recognize the limitations of your own knowledge and perspectives, and be open to learning from others and adapting your understanding as needed. In conclusion, building your sense of right and wrong through books, research, and trusted individuals can lead to informed and thoughtful decision-making. However, it's essential to be aware of the potential pitfalls and take steps to mitigate them. By being mindful of these factors and continually refining your approach, you can make more informed decisions and develop a strong, personal moral framework.
